newsitem.title: GERMANY: Ireland in limelight as Book Fair kicks off.
newsitem.headline: Ireland in limelight as Book Fair kicks off.

text.p: Guinness is flowing in the beer halls of Frankfurt this week as poets and playwrights pour in from Ireland to celebrate the Irish-themed Book Fair, the publishing world's biggest annual get-together.

Giving the event an Irish flavour, authentic "pints of plain" are on tap at the Fair's specially constructed Guinness-sponsored pub, also the focal point for the troop of some 30 Irish writers and 26 publishers in attendance.
Meanwhile, the city's better-established Irish pubs are hoping that the Fair and associated Irish Festival will give a fresh boost to Germany's longstanding enthusiasm for all things Irish.

"I think the Book Fair will put Ireland on the map, not only in Frankfurt but in Germany. It's going to be very, very successful for Ireland," said Tony Dwyer, who runs the popular "Irish Pub" in the centre of Frankfurt.

Irish President Mary Robinson, in Frankfurt on Tuesday for the official launch of the Fair, welcomed German Chancellor Helmut Kohl's plans for a two-day state visit to Ireland this week and said she hoped more Germans would follow suit.
"The Festival will portray a sense of Ireland through our contemporary literature and broader culture, an image that may not be so well known generally," Robinson said.

At least seventeen Irish titles have been translated into German to mark the Fair, among them essays by Nobel Prize winning poet Seamus Heaney, who already generates steady sales here. Music events and art exhibitions with an Irish theme are also scheduled all over the country.

Enthusiasm for Ireland may be reaching a peak this week but German appetite for Irish culture -- especially its beer -- is well established. Frankfurt alone boasts half a dozen Irish bars and new venues open regularly.

"The minute you say you are Irish you get this warmth in the response that people here from England or France just never get," said Cork-born Madeleine O'Byrne, now at the research department of Dresdner Bank in Frankfurt.
But she added: "We Irish can't even get flights home at Christmas because of the competition from the Germans."
